lessons.title: চা (chā) — "tea," and the first word you can politely offer
lessons.gloss: tea — a loanword that crossed from China into Bengali overland, and the drink this chapter's polite offers run on

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Last lesson you said āmār chā bhālo lāge, "I like tea," without চা ever being taught on its own. Here it is, by itself — and a new job for a form you already own.
চা — chā — tea.

চা (chā) is চ (chô) with the vowel sign া (ā). চ is a plain, unaspirated ch, the sound at the start of English church with no puff of breath behind it — Bengali also has a breathy partner, ছ, for later.

চা (chā) is not Sanskrit at all. It came into Bengali from Persian čā, which took it from Chinese chá. That is the overland route: China to Persia to Bengal, the same road Hindi and Punjabi travelled. The words that reached Europe — English tea, French thé — went the opposite way, by sea, from Hokkien Chinese tê, carried on Dutch trading ships. One drink, two ends of the same word, arriving by two different roads.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: an offer, built on a form you already have

segments.text: Chapter 7 taught you আপনি খান (āpni khān), the respectful form of খাওয়া. Put a noun in front of it and the very same words become a polite offer or request:

utterances: Bengali: আপনি খান. what it does: you eat / you drink (respectful).
Bengali: চা (chā) খান. what it does: (please) have some tea.

segments.text: No new ending to learn — চা (chā) খান reuses exactly what Chapter 7 already gave you.

segments.text: Offer someone tea, politely. (চা (chā) খান.) Is চা (chā) inherited from Sanskrit? (No — it is a Chinese word that reached Bengali by way of Persian.) What form does চা (chā) খান reuse? (আপনি খান, Chapter 7's respectful "you eat/drink," with no new ending.)

lessons.title: জল (jôl) — "water," prised out of a phrase you already know
lessons.gloss: water — the word Chapter 7 already used to say "drink water," now taught on its own, beside the Bangladesh-register পানি

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Chapter 7 taught you জল (jôl) খাওয়া, "to drink water" — literally "water-eat" — without ever teaching জল (jôl) by itself. Here it is, on its own.
জল — jôl — water.
জল (jôl) খান — (please) drink some water, the same offer pattern as last lesson.

জল is জ (jô) + ল (l), two bare consonants with no vowel sign between them. জ keeps its inherent vowel; ল, at the end of the word with nothing written after it, is silent — so jôl, one syllable, not jô-lô.

জল (jôl) is Sanskrit জল (jôl) (jala), inherited straight through Prakrit. Past Sanskrit its root is genuinely unsettled: one proposal traces it to PIE gʷelHo-, "to gush forth, to spring" — but the same sources call a local, non-Indo-European origin "unlikely though possible." No confident cousin is claimed here; the honest answer is that nobody is sure.

Bengali has a second word for water, most common in Bangladesh: পানি (pani). That one is on secure ground — Sanskrit pānīya, "drinkable," built directly on √pā, "to drink," the very root behind Chapter 7's পান করা and English potion, potable. Two words for the same thing, one of disputed origin and one you can trace all the way home.

lessons.gloss: milk — a word whose spelling could ask for a trailing vowel but doesn't, and a root whose one secure English cousin is not the word it looks like

segments.text: Chapter 9 met a word that had to end in a vowel nobody wrote — সাহায্য, sāhājjo. This word looks like it could do the same thing. It doesn't.
দুধ — dudh — milk.
দুধ (dudh) খান — (please) have some milk.
দুধ (dudh) is দ (dô) with the vowel sign ু (u), plus ধ (dh), a breathy dental d. Nothing is written after ধ — the same bare-consonant ending সাহায্য had.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: why this one stays silent

segments.text: সাহায্য had to surface its inherent vowel — sāhājjo, not sāhājj — because its final letter is a doubled consonant, য্য, and a bare cluster like that cannot be said at all without a vowel to carry it. দুধ ends in one plain consonant, ধ, which needs no such help. So Bengali leaves it silent: দুধ, not dudho. The spelling looks the same kind of "bare ending" in both words; whether the vowel survives depends on what it would take to pronounce the letter beneath it.

দুধ (dudh) is Sanskrit দুগ্ধ (dugdha), the past participle of √দুহ্ (√duh, "to milk"), from PIE dʰewgʰ-, "to produce, to yield." That root has exactly one secure English descendant, and it is not the word you would guess: doughty, "valiant," through Old English dohtig, "capable, of use." The word that looks like a cousin, dough, is not one — it comes from a completely different PIE root, dʰeyǵʰ-, "to knead, to mould." A close sound, two unrelated histories.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two endings compared — "sāhājjo … dudh"]

segments.text: Why does সাহায্য keep its final vowel while দুধ (dudh) doesn't? (সাহায্য ends in a doubled consonant that cannot be said bare; দুধ (dudh)'s single ধ can.) Is দুধ (dudh)'s root related to English dough? (No — that is a different PIE root; the real cousin is doughty.)

lessons.gloss: cooked rice — the meal itself, and a Sanskrit root for "share" that will resurface two lessons from now in a very different word

segments.text: Three drinks so far. This chapter closes on the word for the meal itself — and a root worth remembering, because it comes back.
ভাত — bhāt — cooked rice.
ভাত (bhāt) খান — (please) eat some rice; in everyday Bengali, "have a meal."

ভাত is ভ (bhô, a b with a puff of breath) with the vowel sign া (ā), plus ত (t), silent at the end for the same reason দুধ (dudh)'s ধ was: a single bare consonant needs no vowel to carry it, so bhāt, not bhāto.

ভাত (bhāt) is Sanskrit ভক্ত (bhakta), "portioned out, shared" — the past participle of √ভজ্ (√bhaj), "to divide, to distribute, to allot." PIE bʰeh₂g- sits behind it. Rice, in this word's own history, is not "the grain" but the share that was given out — the meal as a portion handed to you.
Hold onto that root. Two lessons from now, the very same Sanskrit verb will turn up again, naming someone rather than something.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "bhāt" — cooked rice, no trailing vowel]

segments.text: What does ভাত literally mean, at the root? ("Portioned out, shared" — √bhaj, "to divide.") Offer all four of this chapter's words, politely, in one breath. (Chā khān, jôl khān, dudh khān, bhāt khān.) Why do দুধ and ভাত both drop their final vowel? (Each ends in one plain consonant, easily said bare.) A quick run back through Chapter 7 while you're at it: which verb does Bengali reach for when আছে runs out of future? (হবে.) How many forms of "I come" does a Bengali speaker need, whoever is talking? (One — āmi āsi.) And "you go" to a stranger, versus to a friend? (যান jān, versus যাও jāo.) সাহায্য's doubled letter — said how? (jj, not yy.)
